claims.text: A nanoscale Cu interlayer can act as a transition material between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
Tuning HEA/Cu interface coherency promotes a crossover between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
Cu has relatively high atomic mobility at elevated temperatures.
The elevated-temperature atomic mobility of Cu facilitates diffusion creep in HEA/Cu multilayers.
Coherent bonding of Cu at lower temperatures or higher stresses permits dislocation nucleation and motion.
The initial HEA multilayer may comprise FCC HEA layers with coherent interfaces.
Introducing a controlled-thickness nanoscale Cu interlayer between HEA layers modifies interface coherency.
HEA/Cu interface coherency can be controlled through Cu-layer thickness.
HEA/Cu interface coherency can be controlled through processing parameters.
At higher temperatures or lower applied stresses, Cu diffusivity promotes diffusion-mediated creep.
Controlled Cu-layer thickness and low-temperature conditions can maintain a highly coherent HEA/Cu interface.
At increased stress, dislocation nucleation and motion within a coherent Cu layer become the dominant creep mechanism.
Improving interface coherency or changing temperature and stress will produce a measurable crossover in creep behavior.
The crossover will involve a shift from diffusion creep toward an increased contribution from dislocation creep.
Baseline HEA multilayers without Cu interlayers, or with randomly incoherent interfaces, exhibit monotonic creep dominated solely by one mechanism.
The proposed transition occurs only for nanoscale Cu interlayers within a restricted temperature and stress regime.
Extremely high temperatures or very thick Cu layers may prevent a clear creep-mechanism crossover.
The crossover conditions depend on HEA chemical composition and processing route.
